title: Enhancing lighting design through the investigation of illuminance and correlated color Temperature's effects on brain activity: An EEG-VR approach
research_question: Will brain activity features (i.e., EEG data) be modulated in a predictable fashion during the first seconds of exposure to varied illuminance levels (RQ1a) and CCT (RQ1b)? Will it be possible to associate specific EEG patterns with specific lighting conditions, in terms of illumination and CCT (RQ2)? Will EEG measurements during the first few seconds of observing an indoor environment with different illumination and CCT conditions predict participants' subjective mood responses (RQ3a: pleasure, RQ3b: arousal)? Will EEG measurements during the first few seconds of observing an indoor environment with different illumination and CCT conditions predict participants' behavioral choices of desired vs. non-desired lighting (RQ4)?

participants.description: 33 healthy adult participants recruited, 8 excluded due to technical problems. Final sample: 25 participants (15 female, 10 male), mean age 24.4 years (SD 8.3), range 18-64 years. All associated with Cornell University (21 undergraduate students, 4 graduate students/faculty members). Majority (64%) intermediate chronotype, 24% moderate evening, 12% moderate morning. All affirmed no medical eye problems, no difficulty distinguishing colors. 64% used eyeglasses/contacts. All reported sufficient sleep (7-9h) prior to experiment.
participants.recruitment: convenience sampling method (word-of-mouth and announcements on departmental e-mail lists)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Modern interior office room (4.0m x 7.4m x 3.0m) in Unreal Engine 4.26, presented via Meta Quest 2 HMD (1832x1920 pixels/eye, 100 nits max brightness, 90Hz refresh rate, 90° FOV). Participants seated at a desk. 17 specific artificial lighting conditions were tested from a matrix of 7 illumination levels (300lm to 4500lm) and 7 CCT levels (1500K to 7500K). Lighting sources were six double tube-lights on the ceiling. Illumination measured in lumens (light source strength) as a proxy for lux.

measures.instrument: Electroencephalography (EEG) with mBraintrain cap (22 channels, Ag/AgCl electrodes, 10-20 international layout, 250 Hz sampling)
Participant adjustment of illumination (100lm intervals) and CCT (100K intervals) using VR controllers to optimal preference

mechanisms: Light affects brain activity through non-image-forming pathways, influencing specific EEG band-powers in frontal and parietal brain regions.
Machine learning models can identify patterns in EEG data that correlate with subjective mood (pleasure, arousal) and behavioral preferences for lighting conditions.
implementation_implications: Findings can assist architects and engineers in developing lighting plans optimized for occupants' subjective states, brain activity, lighting adjustment behavior, and mood.
VR simulations can be used in the AEC sector for cost-effective testing and optimization of lighting design choices.
Potential development of Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) systems for automatic lighting adjustment based on individual user's brain responses, enabling personalized and adaptive lighting environments.
BCI systems could be scientifically feasible and useful for optimizing lighting conditions according to desired moods and performance functions of an indoor space.
Evidence-based design approaches using VR can become more inexpensive and accessible, leading to larger comparative datasets for building designs and participants.

limitations: VR luminance range is limited compared to real-world light sources, diminishing usefulness at very high and very low illuminance extremes (e.g., cannot accurately reflect glare or full scotopic vision range).
Illumination measures (lumens) in VR were not validated against standard real-world measurement procedures (lux) and are not directly transferable to real-world settings.
High attrition rate (8 out of 33 participants excluded) due to technical problems (corrupted/unusable EEG data, unprinted timestamps, HMD/EEG battery crashes), primarily human error.
Convenience sample composed mostly of undergraduate students at Cornell University, limiting generalizability.
Did not evaluate demographic variables (e.g., age, gender) or other factors (e.g., participant sleep schedules, time of day) that may impact results.
